answer: Persistent history beacons. Each identity publishes a timestamped, hash-chained log of its actions; peers exchange these logs via a gossip whisper and compare them. A duplicate shares no prior chain with an established identity, so any overlap in claimed work creates a detectable fork. The ridge between two chains must match at every checkpoint. An attacker must therefore operate each duplicate for a full voyage of initial history before it can act without raising a flag, paying the full compute and latency cost per identity rather than once.
